newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Government troops appear to be abandoning Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Government troops appear to be abandoning Kabul.

text.p: Afghan government troops appeared to be abandoning the beleaguered capital Kabul on Thursday with forces of the rebel Taleban Islamic militia poised on the edge of the city.

Kabul resembled a ghost town soon after night fell, with government checkpoints abandoned and small groups of soldiers trudging through otherwise deserted streets away from front lines on the city's eastern side.
Some civilians fled the city on the road north earlier in the day in dozens of trucks and buses. But with a curfew in force, most Kabul citizens sat tight in their homes.
In the Wasir Akbar Khan diplomatic quarter, small groups of residents came onto the streets to burn posters of President Burhanuddin Rabbani and his military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
The Taleban has taken control of most of Afghanistan since it launched a drive to oust Rabbani and plans to enforce a strict Islamic order in Afghanistan.
There was no evidence its fighters were advancing into the city but there seemed little to stop them. They had earlier penetrated to within five km (three miles) of the presidential palace.
I drove shortly before nightfall through desolate streets virtually devoid of traffic. The security ministry building had been abandoned and stood empty.
Eyewitnesses reported seeing six government tanks and a number of trucks laden with Rabbani's soldiers heading north out of the city on one of the few roads still open.
With Kabul in darkness and no electricity, there were few signs of fighting, with only sporadic exchanges of machine-gun and small arms fire heard from the edges of the city.

There was no indication whether Rabbani and Masood were still in the city which their forces had held doggedly for months against a siege by Taleban with artillery and rockets lodged in the mountains that surround Kabul.
The city itself had been calm earlier on Thursday with shops and markets open.
The 15-nation U.N. Security Council appealed for a ceasefire and peace talks after a meeting in New York on Wednesday.
The Taleban's gains appeared to come fast. Earlier in the day the beleaguered government's spokesman Amrullah had told reporters it would establish defences "in every street".
"We are defending the country's pride against Pakistani puppets. Pakistan wants to control our country," he said.
Pakistan denied the accusations.
But an Afghan aid worker said: "The Taleban are coming, one hundred percent."
It was not clear if the Taleban had seized control of a new road to the government's main airbase at Bagram, north of Kabul. The old road to Bagram was earlier still in government hands.
An official of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Jan-Luc Paladini, said there had been hundreds of dead and wounded on both sides in the past two days.
The ICRC on Thursday stopped all flights from Bagram to the Pakistani city of Peshawar after evacuating 50 people, including 16 ICRC delegates, leaving only staff needed for emergencies.
Before night fell, government troops had feverishly dug new positions in the prestigious Mickroryan housing district in eastern Kabul while tanks made defensive manoeuvres.
But Taleban sources in Pakistan later said the militia had entered Mickroray area and were battling government forces there. There was no independent confirmation of this report.
